key_concept: The self-inductance of a long solenoid is $L = \mu_0 n^2 A l$, found from the flux linkage $N\Phi = LI$ with a uniform internal field $B = \mu_0 n I$.
steps: Let a current $I$ flow in the solenoid. The field inside a long solenoid is uniform: $B = \mu_0 n I$.
The cross-sectional area is $A = \pi r^2$, so the flux through one turn is $\Phi_1 = BA = \mu_0 n I \pi r^2$.
The total number of turns is $N = nl$, so the total flux linkage is $N\Phi_1 = (nl)(\mu_0 n I \pi r^2) = \mu_0 \pi n^2 r^2 l\, I$.
Using $N\Phi_1 = LI$ gives $L = \mu_0 \pi n^2 r^2 l$.
Check: $\mu_0 n^2 \times (\text{volume } \pi r^2 l)$ has units of $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}} \times \mathrm{m^{-2}} \times \mathrm{m^3} = \mathrm{H}$, as required.
why_not_others: Option (2) drops the $\pi$ by using $r^2$ instead of the area $\pi r^2$. Options (3) and (4) bring in the $2\pi$ factors that belong to straight-wire or circular-loop field formulas, not to the solenoid.
common_trap: Students often multiply by $n$ only once (giving $\mu_0 n r^2 \pi l$) or forget the $\pi$ in the area, instead of using total turns $N = nl$ together with $B = \mu_0 n I$.
time_saving_tip: Remember $L = \mu_0 n^2 \times (\text{volume of solenoid})$; with volume $= \pi r^2 l$, option (1) follows at once.
